Banks should maintain an auditable record showing that important notices were sent and delivered to customers.

A practical approach is to track every notice as an auditable event. Whether it's sent by email, WhatsApp, download, or print, each action is recorded with a timestamp. If a third-party delivery provider is used, the delivery or tracking ID is also logged, creating a complete proof-of-delivery trail for audits and compliance.

Although the DPDP Act does not specifically require a
, maintaining compliance documentation is considered a best practice.

Organizations should retain records such as consent logs, privacy notices, data inventories, retention schedules, security policies, vendor agreements, breach response documentation, and Data Principal request logs. These records help demonstrate accountability and simplify audits, investigations, and internal compliance reviews.
In most cases, the
Data Fiduciary remains accountable
under the DPDP Act, even if a data breach occurs at a third-party Data Processor or reseller. Sharing personal data with a third party does not transfer your responsibility for protecting it.
To reduce your risk, establish clear responsibilities before sharing any personal data. A well-defined
Data Processing Agreement (DPA)
should outline each party's security obligations, breach notification timelines, and liability in the event of a security incident.

Restaurants often collect a customer's mobile number or email for order updates, loyalty programs, or marketing. Under the
DPDP Act
, customers should be informed about why their personal data is being collected before they share it.
There are two practical ways to do this:
Self-service kiosk or tablet:

Let customers enter their own mobile number or email on a customer-facing screen that clearly explains the purpose of data collection. This ensures the customer is informed at the point of collection, and their consent is captured at the same time.
Printed privacy notice:

If a self-service screen isn't available, display a privacy notice at the counter explaining why the data is being collected and how long it will be retained before staff ask for the customer's details.

Under the DPDP Act, hotels are responsible for handling guests' personal information securely. Collecting government-issued ID documents through a staff member's personal phone or WhatsApp creates unnecessary privacy risks, as there is no centralized storage, limited access control, or reliable audit trail to demonstrate how the information was handled.
A more secure approach is to
digitize the check-in process by allowing guests to upload their ID through a secure digital form.

The document is stored directly in a centralized, access-controlled repository instead of passing through personal devices. This ensures only authorized staff can access the document, while every upload and access is logged for audit purposes.

Data Fiduciary
is the person or organization that decides why and how personal data will be processed.
For example, when an online store
collects
your name, address, and contact details to deliver an order, the store is the Data Fiduciary.

of the Act states that this role comes with responsibilities, including giving proper notice, taking reasonable security safeguards, responding to Data Principal requests, and
reporting personal data

No. Although both roles deal with privacy matters, they have different responsibilities under the DPDP Act.

Every Data Fiduciary must publish the contact details of a person who can handle Data Principal queries and grievances. A Data Protection Officer (DPO) is a separate role that's required only for organizations notified as Significant Data Fiduciaries (SDFs). The DPO must be based in India, report to the organization's Board, and act as the primary point of contact with the Data Protection Board, in addition to overseeing grievance handling.

The definition is provided under
Section 2(j)
of the Act. A
Data Principal
is the individual to whom personal data relates. In simple terms, if an organization
collects or uses
your name, email address, phone number, or other personal information, you are the Data Principal.
The term also covers a
parent or lawful guardian
acting on behalf of a child, and a lawful guardian acting on behalf of a person with a disability.
As a
Data Principal
, you have rights under the DPDP Act, such as the right to access information about your personal data, request correction or erasure, and raise grievances.

Not necessarily. The DPDP Act recognizes that certain processing activities are necessary even without consent. Under Section 7, organizations can process personal data for legitimate uses such as fraud prevention, detecting or investigating offences, and maintaining information security.

This isn't a blanket exemption from the rest of the Act. Organizations must still ensure the processing is proportionate, limited to its intended purpose, and supported by appropriate security safeguards. Where consent isn't the legal basis, it's still important to maintain clear records demonstrating why the data was processed under the legitimate-use provision.
